units.text: Choose a database by the questions the application needs to answer, not the name of the service. Joining orders to customers and committing a payment fit a relational engine. Looking up an order by its known key fits DynamoDB when the access patterns are planned.

Nested documents point toward a document database. Time-series queries need a suitable time-series engine and A P I. Search ranking belongs in a search index, and repeated hot reads may benefit from a cache. In either case, preserve the authoritative data store.
Before choosing, validate consistency, capacity and recovery. Ask how much data you can lose and how quickly the application needs to be restored.

Use Amazon R D S when you want a managed relational engine but still need to design the database. The application connects to an endpoint and engine port. The security group is the network gate. The instance runs the chosen engine and uses the configured compute, storage and parameter group.

The database subnet group identifies eligible subnets, normally across at least two Availability Zones. A standard single-instance deployment still runs in one zone at a time. Multi-A Z is a separate availability choice.
Standard R D S does not give direct host access; R D S Custom differs. Plan database permissions and tune queries inside the engine. Growing storage does not fix a compute or query bottleneck.
R D S manages infrastructure work, not your database design. AWS provisions and maintains the platform, handles supported patching and automated backups, and monitors infrastructure health.

You still choose the engine and configuration, design schemas and indexes, assign database permissions, and tune queries. You also pick capacity for the workload rather than assuming the managed service sizes it for you.

In the storage example, the instance starts at one hundred gibibytes and can grow within a configured maximum. Storage autoscaling does not shrink it automatically, and it does not fix C P U pressure, connection limits, or slow S Q L.

An R D S connection needs network reachability and database authorization. The Lambda function finds the private database endpoint through D N S and routing. The security group permits the engine port. That only gets the client to the database or proxy.

In this example the orders A P I reaches port five four three two. T L S protects the connection when configured or required. The database authenticates app reader, and the database grant allows select. The query returns the order row because each layer succeeds.
If the port is unreachable, check the network. If login fails or select is denied, check the corresponding database layer. An open port does not grant S Q L access.

Choose backups when you need to recover a prior state. R D S automated backups and transaction logs let you choose a point in time within the retention window. The restore creates a new database; it does not rewind production in place.
A manual snapshot is a deliberate recovery point that remains until it is deleted. For a supported cross-account or cross-Region copy, include encryption-key permissions in the plan.
A read replica serves traffic and is not backup history. Validate the restored data, permissions and endpoint, then cut over only after the application passes its checks.

Choose a classic Multi-A Z DB instance standby for availability, not read scaling. The primary replicates synchronously to a non-readable standby. When R D S fails over, the application reconnects using the database endpoint.

Choose read replicas for a separate read path. Replication to these replicas is asynchronous; application reads can see lag. The example shows a same-Region reader and, where supported, a reader in another Region.
Availability, query scaling and recovery are different goals. Test failover or promotion and how your clients reconnect instead of treating a replica as interchangeable with a standby.

Choose between the two Multi-A Z designs by read and failover requirements. The classic DB instance deployment sends reads and writes to the primary. Its synchronous standby protects availability without accepting application read traffic.

In a supported Multi-A Z DB cluster deployment, send writes to the writer endpoint and reads to the reader endpoint. The cluster uses semisynchronous replication, with two readable DB instances in separate zones.
Do not infer read capacity from the Multi-A Z name alone. Check the engine and supported deployment, expected failover behavior, cost, and whether application reads actually use the reader endpoint.

Use weighted D N S to influence fresh answers, not to split S Q L queries exactly. Here Route 53 chooses among reader destinations on a new lookup, with weights 80 and 20. The answer can be cached until its time to live expires.

A connection pool keeps using open connections. New connections may still use a cached answer. The reader options are for reads; writes still go to the primary. An 80 to 20 weight is not a promise about the query count.
Measure observed connections, query load and replication lag per reader. If workload share differs from the D N S weights, check caching, connection reuse and the application before changing weights.

Protect R D S at three separate layers: encryption at rest, T L S in transit, and logs for audit. For a database connection, verify the server certificate rather than relying only on an encrypted socket.
Use AWS K M S to encrypt stored R D S data and its snapshots. If you have an unencrypted snapshot, copy it with encryption, then restore the copy as a new encrypted database.

Use CloudTrail for R D S service A P I actions, and configure database engine auditing or query logs for S Q L activity. Oracle or S Q L Server transparent data encryption, where supported, is a separate engine feature.
Use I A M database authentication for a temporary login, not to grant S Q L access. Enable it on a supported engine and configure a matching database user with only the S Q L grants it needs.
The I A M principal needs R D S D B connect. Generate a Signature Version four token for the exact endpoint, port, and database user, then connect over T L S.
The token is valid for fifteen minutes for login. Expiry does not end an existing session. If the login succeeds but a SELECT fails, check the database grants, not the token.

Choose the recovery artifact by the destination. For a managed R D S target, restore the snapshot or use a point-in-time restore from automated backups. Both paths create a new instance; validate the application before switching.
For a supported move to self-managed Oracle, use an eligible R Man backup made through the R D S admin procedures. Transfer supported backup files through S three and restore them on the Oracle host.

Check the Oracle versions, backup format, and transparent data encryption support before choosing the route. Managed R D S does not give you host access or S Y S privileges, and it does not support Oracle R A C.

Move MySQL in three phases so the target can catch up before accepting writes. Seed it from a consistent export, then replicate subsequent changes with a supported binary log or G T I D configuration.
Keep writes on the source during catch-up. At cutover, pause source writes, confirm lag and errors are clear, validate the data and application, then switch the application to the target.

Rollback is simplest before the target accepts writes. After target writes begin, stop them and reconcile those target-only changes, using tested reverse replication or the recovery plan, before routing back.
Use R D S Proxy when application connection bursts strain the database. Many client sessions can share fewer database connections, so the proxy reduces connection overhead without fixing slow S Q L.
The proxy and its database stay in the same V P C. A client from another V P C can use an additional private proxy endpoint in that client V P C, within the same Region.
Configure both authentication hops separately: client to proxy, then proxy to database. Session pinning reduces connection reuse; database capacity and connection borrowing limits still apply.
Route writes and reads to separate proxy endpoints only when the target has real readers. In this Aurora cluster, the application’s write pool uses the default endpoint to reach the writer.
The read-only pool uses a reader endpoint to reach eligible readers in the same cluster. Creating an endpoint does not create a replica or attach a proxy to a standalone R D S read replica.
Before relying on the read path, verify the engine and configuration, reader health, replication lag, and how session pinning affects connection reuse.

Treat a cross-Region outage as a cutover, not like an in-Region availability-zone failover. In this supported design, changes are copied asynchronously, so recent writes may not have reached the second Region.

Check the replication lag against your data-loss tolerance. Fence the old writer and verify it cannot receive writes. Then promote and validate the replica before switching the application endpoint and reconnecting.

The recovery point objective is the acceptable data loss. The recovery time objective is the target restoration time. A same-Region Multi A Z D B instance instead fails over automatically and clients reconnect to the same endpoint.
